name: Private Blockchain
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Private Blockchains: One Organization, One Ledger
lesson.summary: A private blockchain is a permissioned network controlled by a single organization, which decides who may read, write, or validate, trading decentralization for internal control and auditability.
lesson.body:
A private blockchain is a permissioned blockchain where a single organization sits at the top of the access hierarchy, deciding who may read the ledger, submit transactions, or run validating nodes. Unlike the permissioned networks discussed generally in an earlier chapter, which could in principle be governed by any defined set of parties, a private blockchain narrows that governance down to one company or institution making the calls alone.

A natural use case is a company that wants to track its own internal records, such as a supply chain, inventory movements across warehouses, or an internal audit trail, using a structure that resists tampering, without opening any part of the system to outside participants. The organization runs all the validating nodes itself, perhaps distributed across different departments or data centers for redundancy, but control never leaves the company's hands.

This raises an obvious question worth sitting with: if one organization controls everything, why use a blockchain at all rather than an ordinary database? The honest answer is that the blockchain's structural properties, cryptographically hash linked blocks that make past records tamper evident, still provide value even within a single organization. If several departments each run a node and cross check the same chain, it becomes much harder for a single rogue employee, or a single compromised server, to quietly alter historical records without the inconsistency being detected by the other nodes. A well designed traditional database with strong access logging and cryptographic signing can achieve something similar, but a private blockchain builds tamper evidence into the data structure itself rather than relying entirely on separate audit tooling layered on top.

That said, skeptics have a fair point here, and it is worth stating plainly rather than glossing over. The decentralized trust that motivates public, permissionless blockchains like Bitcoin, namely that no single party can unilaterally rewrite the rules or the history, is largely absent in a private blockchain. The controlling organization can, in principle, change the software, override validators, or restart the chain from an earlier state, because it is the same entity that authorized every node in the first place. A private blockchain buys internal tamper evidence and a structured audit trail, not the trustlessness that makes public blockchains interesting to people who do not trust the operator at all.

This limitation is exactly why some organizations look past private blockchains toward arrangements that spread control across more than one party, without going all the way to a fully open, permissionless network. That middle ground, where several independent organizations share governance rather than one company holding it alone, is the subject of the next chapter on consortium blockchains.
